newsitem.title: CHINA: S.Korea begins shipping Red Cross food to North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea begins shipping Red Cross food to North.

text.p: Trains carrying the first shipments of a landmark 50,000 tonnes of food aid from South Korea have begun rumbling over the border from China to Seoul's famine-threatened Northern rival, officials said on Thursday.
It was the first time South Korean Red Cross officials had entered the North in 12 years.

Transport had begun of a first batch of 11,200 tonnes of donated corn and flour organised by the South Korean Red Cross under an accord hammered out last month between Seoul and Pyongyang, said a South Korean embassy spokesman in Beijing.
"This is the first batch since the Red Cross talks," said spokesman Chang Moon-ik.

Transportation difficulties meant it was not yet clear how long it would take to transport the first batch, but Seoul was already planning a second batch of 16,000 tonnes to be shipped between June 20-27, Chang said.

"Altogether nine persons of the (South) Korean Red Cross team have already visited North Korea," he said, adding that team members on Thursday held a ceremony to mark their arrival on the Northern side of the border.

The South Korean Red Cross has promised to supply 50,000 tonnes of corn, flour, powdered milk and instant noodles to the hungry North by the end of July. The Red Cross last went to North Korea in 1985 to help displaced families visit their hometowns.
A railway manager in the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong said a first shipment of 600 tonnes of cornflour trundled across the nearby border to North Korea on Wednesday.

Red Cross officials had been unable to confirm how much food would be shipped through Dandong, since the cornflour was being brought from other areas of northeastern China, the railway manager said by telephone.
"We are waiting for more to arrive, then we will take it across," he said. "However much comes, that's how much we will ship."

He said the corn flour shipments carried across the Yalu River border between China and its Stalinist hermit neighbour had been clearly labelled as coming from the South Korean Red Cross -- a key condition imposed by Seoul under the aid accord.

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since their 1950-53 war ended only in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even donations of food a delicate diplomatic affair.

Apart from Dandong, South Korean officials were also arranging shipments through two other approved border towns, Ji'an and Tumen, spokesman Chang said. Under the North-South accord the aid can also be shipped by sea to selected ports.
International aid agencies have warned that North Korea desperately needs large-scale food aid to avert severe famine caused by years of economic decline and natural disasters.
A senior South Korean official on Wednesday accused North Korea of manipulating data to exaggerate its hunger and deprivation in a bid to secure international help.
Vice National Unification Minister Kim Suk-woo said Pyongyang faced acute food shortages but warnings of imminent famine were exaggerated.
Seoul would not rush to help its Cold War rival until the North took action -- such as cutting military spending -- to solve its chronic food problems, Kim said.
